topics.name: Too ... to / so ... that / enough to

options: Riya is tall enough to reach the shelf.
Riya is enough tall to reach the shelf.
Riya is tall enough reach the shelf.
questions.rule: Enough comes after an adjective (tall enough) and is followed by to + verb.

options: If you works hard, you will win.
If you work hard, you will won.
If you work hard, you will win.
questions.rule: Type 1: If + simple present, will + base verb. 'you' takes work; will is followed by win.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: enough to is followed by the base verb: old enough to drive.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Passive after will be needs the past participle: will be cancelled.

questions.after: hunger could stop the brave climber.
questions.rule: Neither always pairs with nor.

questions.after: heavy that the child could not lift it.
questions.rule: so + adjective + that + clause: so heavy that ...
Question: Is + subject + adjective + enough.

chat: Will you come to the market with me?
options: If I will finish my homework, I come.
If I finished my homework, I will coming.
If I finish my homework, I will come.
questions.rule: Type 1: If + simple present (finish), main clause will + base verb (will come).

chat: Are you ready for the race?
questions.rule: Present perfect needs the past participle practised; enough comes after the verb here.

questions.source: Meena is too tired to walk.
options: Meena is so tired that she can walk.
Meena is so tired that she cannot walk.
Meena is too tired that she cannot walk.
questions.rule: too ... to = so ... that + negative: so tired that she cannot walk.

options: Neither the coach nor the players was ready.
Neither the coach or the players were ready.
Neither the coach nor the players were ready.
questions.rule: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: players were.

options: Unless you practise, you will not improve.
Unless you don't practise, you will not improve.
Unless you practise, you will not improved.
questions.rule: Unless already means 'if not', so don't add another not.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: enough + countable noun takes the plural: enough seats.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: If I were you (imaginary) takes would in the main clause.
With either ... or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: sisters are.
time is uncountable, so use enough; many and a few go with countable nouns.
If-clause (simple present) + comma + an instruction (imperative): work hard.

chat: Did Sahil or Neha bring the charts?
options: Neither of them bring the charts.
Neither of them brings the charts yesterday.
Neither of them brought the charts.
questions.rule: The question is in the past (Did), so reply in the simple past: brought.

questions.source: The ladder is so tall that it can reach the roof.
options: The ladder is enough tall to reach the roof.
The ladder is tall enough to reach the roof.
The ladder is tall enough reaching the roof.
questions.rule: so ... that ... can = adjective + enough to + verb: tall enough to reach.

questions.source: If you do not hurry, you will miss the train.
options: Unless you do not hurry, you will miss the train.
Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.
Unless you hurry, you missed the train.
questions.rule: If ... not becomes Unless + positive verb; keep the main clause the same.

options: The tea was too hot for me to drink it.
The tea was too hot that I could not drink.
The tea was too hot for me to drink.
questions.rule: After too ... to, don't repeat the object (no 'it'); 'too' never goes with 'that'.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Neither Asha nor Meera = not one, not the other; the nearer subject (Meera) is singular: is.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: too ... to + base verb: too weak to stand.
Type 1: the if-clause takes the simple present (works), not will.
Adjective + enough to shows something is possible: clever enough to solve.
too + adjective + for + person + to + verb.

chat: What would you do if you won a lakh rupees?
options: If I win a lakh, I would bought a telescope.
I would buy a telescope for our school.
I will bought a telescope for our school.
questions.rule: An imaginary question (would ... if you won) takes would + base verb: would buy.

chat: Why didn't you buy the shoes?
options: They were not cheap enough for me.
They were not enough cheap for me.
They were not cheaply enough for me.
questions.rule: Adjective first, then enough: cheap enough. After 'were' use the adjective, not the adverb.

questions.source: Cold did not stop him, and hunger did not stop him.
options: Neither cold nor hunger stopped him.
Neither cold or hunger stopped him.
Neither cold nor hunger did not stop him.
questions.rule: Neither ... nor is already negative, so the verb is positive: stopped.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: 'you' takes want (no -s); will is followed by the base verb achieve.

options: Last year Tara is not old enough to join the team.
Last year Tara was not old enough to join the team.
Last year Tara was not enough old to join the team.
questions.rule: Last year needs the past (was); enough follows the adjective: old enough.

options: Either you or Rahul have to clear the stage.
Either you nor Rahul has to clear the stage.
Either you or Rahul has to clear the stage.
questions.rule: Either ... or: verb agrees with the nearer subject (Rahul): has. Either pairs with or.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A time clause about the future uses the simple present, and 'Shreya' is singular: begins.

questions.before: The poet had worked so hard
questions.rule: so + adverb/adjective is completed by that + result.
enough comes before a noun: enough money. Question: Do + you + have.

chat: Shall we go for the movie or the match?
options: Neither. I am too tired that I cannot go out.
Neither. I am too tired to go out.
Neither. I am so tired to go out.
questions.rule: Use too ... to or so ... that; never mix them (too ... that, so ... to).

options: He was not enough fit, so the coach rested him.
He was not fit enough, so the coach rest him.
He was not fit enough, so the coach rested him.
questions.rule: fit enough (adjective + enough), and keep the past tense: the coach rested him.

questions.source: The question was too difficult for the students to answer.
options: The question was so difficult that the students cannot answer it.
The question was so difficult that the students could answer it.
The question was so difficult that the students could not answer it.
questions.rule: too ... to = so ... that ... not; keep the past tense (could not) and add the object it.

questions.source: Unless you are confident, you cannot win.
options: If you are confident, you cannot win.
If you are not confident, you cannot won.
If you are not confident, you cannot win.
questions.rule: Unless = if ... not: If you are not confident ...

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this message.
questions.rule: Neither Sameer nor Ravi (singular) was; too ... to + base verb: to run.

options: If you will be brave enough to try, nothing can keep you away from your goal.
If you are brave enough to try, nothing can keep you away from your goal.
If you are enough brave to try, nothing can keep you away from your goal.
questions.rule: No will in the if-clause; adjective before enough: brave enough.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The subject nearer the verb is the many hours (plural), so use were.

questions.after: harder last year, he would have won the medal.
questions.rule: Type 3 (past, unreal): If + past perfect (had trained), would have + past participle.
Question: Was + subject + adjective + enough to + verb.

options: If I had woken up earlier, I would have caught it.
If I woke up earlier, I would have caught it.
If I had woken up earlier, I would catch it yesterday.
questions.rule: A regret about the past: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

questions.source: The problem is so easy that a child can solve it.
options: The problem is easy enough for a child to solve.
The problem is enough easy for a child to solve.
The problem is too easy for a child to solve.
questions.rule: so ... that ... can = adjective + enough for ... to; drop the object 'it'. 'enough' follows the adjective; 'too easy' changes the meaning.

questions.source: If Mira had trained regularly, she would have won.
options: Had Mira train regularly, she would have won.
Had Mira trained regularly, she would have won.
Had Mira trained regularly, she will have won.
questions.rule: Drop If and put Had first: Had Mira trained ..., she would have won.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: a person wants; neither ... nor pain (singular) stops; too ... to + base verb: to give up.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: to + base verb: to leave; will celebrate; nearer subject 'players' is plural: are.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this message.
questions.rule: enough to solve; will become; after a preposition use the object pronoun: proud of him.
